articles.content:
Latin-America and European cinema triumphed at Friday’s awards ceremony of Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival whose fame for discoveries was born out one more year by its final winners, including in its industry section.

For her first year as Artistic Director, Trinn Tramberg had prioritized mixing second time directors with established names in the official selection, a bet which looks to have paid off. The biggest award at Tallinn Black Nights, known as PÖFF, the €20,000 ($22,00) Grand Prix from the City of Tallinn was handed out by a jury chaired by Sir Christopher Hampton ,to “On Top of the Cliff,” he sophomore feature from Peruvian-born Enrica Perez (“Climas)”. Its lead, newcomer Bianca Bucelli, also earned a best actress nod. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The co-production between Perú, Mexico and Switzerland is a psycho thriller about faith, obsession and control, set within a secluded Catholic girls’ boarding school on the cliffs of 1950’s Lima. Reason8 handles sales.

“Among a number of extremely accomplished entries, the jury was especially impressed by the high quality of every department of this film – direction, script, acting, cinematography, design and music – combining to create a hermetic universe, intense, powerful and visually eloquent,” said the jury.

Another second timer female helmer – Germany’s Alison Kuhn – was hailed for her script of “The Matriarch.” The first film with an almost exclusively Vietnamese-German cast, was praised for its “immersion in a community rarely represented on screen, and its nuanced and sensitive exploration of a mother-daughter relationship that navigates the blurred boundaries between right and wrong, care and cruelty, and the harsh rules imposed by the need to survive.” Pluto Films is its sales agent. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Making his screen debut in “The Assignment” by seasoned Belgian helmer Patrice Toy, Mathisse De Sutter was singled out in the acting category for “his ability to depict the tenderness and emotional depth he brought to a story about masculinity in the aftermath of war.”

Two buzzy titles were distinguished for their craft achievements: Patricia Ortega’s biopic “Caballé” -flagship title of the Basque region’s Special Focus in Tallinn and Ireland’s “One Sweet Hour” by Declan Recks. Within the highly competitive First Feature slot, the top win went to the anti-Taliban female-driven pic “ When She Hears the Bells ” by Chabname Zariab headlined by Golshifteh Farahani. “It is a tense, emotional story of resistance and courage that kept us on the edge of our seats. We were hugely impressed to see a debut with such scale and energy and congratulate the filmmakers on a vital story that will stay with us for a long time, said the jury headed by seasoned producer Ivana MacKinnon (“How to Have Sex”).

Established Danish docu helmer and war reporter Naieb Khaja took best director for his debut fiction “Lionheart” set in Copenhagen’s gang scene, while Polish helmer Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s “Exotic” picked a split Special Jury Prize. “The tender, human and generous film got under our skin and gave us access to a unique world. We had a great time watching this film!” said the jury about the pic set in the pole dancing community. Pluto Film handles sales.

In the boundary-pushing section Rebels with a Cause, overseen by Javier Garcia Puerto, the top honor went to the US indie “Pop Pop” by Dylan Stephen Levers, produced by the helmer with W. Ian Ross and Consuelo Althouse.

“Made with an undeniable independent spirit, you can feel the sheer determination of its filmmakers to will this work into existence. Urgent, vital, and unafraid to challenge, this is exactly the kind of rebellious filmmaking we need more than ever in these divisive times,” said the jurors Jason Wood, Samuel Abrahams, Mireia Vilapuig.

Meanwhile in the Critics’ Picks curated by the well-known Nikolaj Nikitin, the top prize went to Bulgarian helmer Maya Vitkova-Kosev (“Viktoria”) for “One Month, a work which jurors Heike-Melba Fendel, Jurgis Matulevičius and Hakim Zejjari said will “most certainly remain in our minds and in our hearts.”

Baltic Blast In a year where the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were under the limelight, gloriously celebrated at the festival which turned 30, some of the region’s brightest stars were profusely applauded tonight at Tallinn’s Alexela Concert Hall. Projects pitched at the Industry & Tallinn & Baltic Event also topped the award list. Lithuania’s newcomer Danielus Minkevicius share a Jury Special Award from the First Feature competition for “Oblivion,” which played for the jurors as “an intimate, deeply moving work from a bold new voice in Baltic cinema.”

In the Baltic competition section, three titles which played at earlier festivals impressed Tallinn’s jury: the Sundance winner and Lithuania’s Oscar hopeful “How to Divorce During the War” by Andrius Blaževičius’ won best film, Latvia’s top helmer Linda Olte best directing for “The Child” while the Cannes Special Screening “Vesna” won a nod for its Baltic co-producers, Stasys Baltakis and Helena Pokorny.

In the doc section which included several minority Baltic co-productions, Spanish helmers Pepe Andreu and Rafa Molés won best film for “La Pietà,” co-produced with Iceland and Lithuania, and a special nod went to Latvia’s “Riga My Love” by Karolina Peterson.

In the Co-Production Market, the project “Wild Love” from Lithuanian genre specialist Jonas Trukana bagged the coveted €20,000 Eurimages Co-Production Development Award for “its audacity to go beyond genre conventions, to convey a timely message, and for the ambition to unite a region behind common values such as care, integrity, independence and sense of humour,” said jurors Stefan Prohorov, Holly Daniel and Ivo Felt. The project produced by Klementina Remeikaitė & Rūta Kiaupaitė for Afterschool also won the Apostlab Scholarship.

Slava Ukraine As always since the start of war in Ukraine, the country and its inspiring people were at the core of PÖFF’s closing act. Ukraine Film Agency’s head Andrii Osipov solemnly awarded PÖFF’s founder Tiina Lokk the Ukraine’s Order of Princess Olga, Third Class, in recognition of her support for Ukrainian cinema and its international promotion. articles.title: 'I Play Rocky' Fact vs Fiction: Butkus the Dog, Bloody Knuckles and Stallone's Fight to Get 'Rocky' Made
articles.summary: The beloved classic “Rocky” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “I Play Rocky,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconic lead role of boxer Rocky Balboa, culminating in a best picture […]
articles.content:
The beloved classic “ Rocky ” premiered half a century ago this week. Five decades later, “ I Play Rocky ,” in theaters now, tells the story of how unknown writer and actor Sylvester Stallone shoulders his way into not just writing the script but playing the iconic lead role of boxer Rocky Balboa, culminating in a best picture Oscar.

In the year 2026, is it really possible to go back in time and depict the making of “Rocky” with perfect accuracy? The unvarnished truth doesn’t always make for the best dramatic impact in a movie — and Stallone and the filmmaking team have told somewhat varying stories over the past 50 years. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Including the Original X-Men ‘Just Felt Right,’ Says Kevin Feige: It's a 'Fun Way to Culminate' 25 Years Abdul El-Sayed Mocks Trump and Ted Cruz's Cruel Rhetoric on 'The View,' Jokes He Wants 'Jihadist Leprechaun' Printed on a Hat

“I Play Rocky” effectively toes the line between hitting most of the events of the production with some degree of accuracy and buffing up others for the sake of more effective storytelling.

Here are some of the scenes that happened just as “I Play Rocky” depicts them — according to most participants — and a few others that use a healthy amount of dramatic license.

Did Stallone really write “Rocky” in three days and then turn down hundreds of thousands so he could star?

“I Play Rocky” shows Anthony Ippolito as Stallone marching into Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler’s office and playing hardball with the big Hollywood producers, hearing offers of more and more money to give up his starring role until the producers finally agree. The need for a tidy narrative leaves out several details, though, and makes Stallone seem like even more of a total unknown than he was at the time.

The real story was a bit more complicated and left out the pivotal role that talent agents typically play in Hollywood deal negotiations. Chris Rumar, the son of one of Stallone's early agents, Craig Rumar, said his dad and Rumar's agent partner Larry Kubik were integral to getting “Rocky” off the ground. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“Since my dad died nine years ago, Mr. Stallone has been on sort of a tour about these inaccuracies about how ‘Rocky’ was put together,” Rumar tells Variety . “This time it was the triple whammy — we got the book, ‘The Steps,’ ‘I Play Rocky’ and the rerelease of ‘Rocky’ all within a month. He has been doing interviews with some of the biggest names in media and nobody challenges him.”

Kubik explained on the "Sexy Boomer" podcast that he and Rumar helped plant the seed for “Rocky” by introducing his friend, producer Gene Kirkwood, who had a deal with Chartoff and Winkler, to Stallone. Kirkwood and the agents first tried to set up Stallone’s script “Hell’s Kitchen” (which later became “Paradise Alley”), but Stallone had already sold it to another company and was trying to double-dip. So he went home and started work on another screenplay, influenced by a boxing match he had watched.

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” Stallone did work day and night for 72 hours to sketch out the basics of the script about an aspiring boxer, with his wife typing up his handwritten lines. But he didn't write a fully-formed screenplay that fast — he sketched out the first third or so of the story, then made dozens of revisions before it was ready to shoot.

The neophyte actor insisted on starring in the movie he wrote — an idea which seemed preposterous to the studio, which would have preferred James Caan, Nick Nolte or Ryan O'Neal. “We negotiated a deal, and in the first deal he got paid for the script,” Kubik said. “I was told by United Artists that Mike Medavoy loved the script. But he loves it for Jimmy Caan. So I said, ‘That is not going to happen.’”

As seen in “I Play Rocky,” United Artists reportedly did offer up to $250,000 if Stallone would step aside, but “Stallone held his ground,” Variety reported. Did he ever deliver the titular line “I play Rocky” to the producers during the discussion of who should star? It's not clear if anyone can remember.

Did Stallone really sell his bull mastiff Butkus for $40 when he was broke, and then buy him back?

In “I Play Rocky,” Stallone treasures the stray dog he found on the street during one of his lowest periods. After moving to Los Angeles, he's still struggling to make ends meet, and sadly decides to sell Butkus to a stranger who compliments the dog for some $40. As Stallone often recounts and as seen in “I Play Rocky,” when it comes time to shoot “Rocky,” Stallone wants Butkus to be in the movie, so he tracks down the new owner, who says his kids love the dog, and ends up having to offer him thousands of dollars (the story varies from $1,500 to $15,000) to buy him back. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Stallone has told a version of the Butkus story many times over the years, naming a man called "Little Jimmy" as the one who bought the dog when he was broke. Stallone implies Little Jimmy was a stranger he met in front of a 7-11, before he sold the "Rocky" script.

But Jimmy Gambina, a diminutive boxing trainer who worked on "Rocky," has a much different recollection of what happened. Gambina told “Going the Distance” author Mike Sielski that he dog-sat for Butkus during the movie's production, and then Stallone gave Gambina the dog after his son Sage was born because he saw how close they had become.

When it was time to shoot “Rocky II,” Stallone wanted the dog back so he could appear in the movie. Gambina says he told Stallone, “You come over and explain it to my son. If my son says it’s OK, I’ll let you have the dog back. But we’ve had the dog going on three years now, and we love the dog.” Gambina says the two had a falling-out sometime after Stallone insisted on taking the dog back.

Did Stallone break his knuckles on a frozen meat carcass at a Philadelphia meat packing facility during filming?

Many people think “Rocky” was shot all in Philadelphia. But only the iconic steps, Rocky's apartment and some other exteriors were captured in the City of Brotherly Love over a frenetic five-day period. “I Play Rocky” shows Stallone’s Rocky Balboa training with sides of beef at a Philly slaughterhouse, but the 1976 original was actually shot at Shamrock Meats in the L.A.-adjacent meat mecca of Vernon. The beef was frozen solid, though, and after Stallone pummeled the icy meat for eight hours straight, he ended up breaking a knuckle, so that part of the movie is accurate.

The ice skating rink where Rocky woos Adrian after hours was the Ice Capades Chalet in Santa Monica, Calif., which later became a Fred Segal store, while the climactic boxing match was filmed at the Olympic Auditorium and the L.A. Sports Arena.

“To help keep budget down, Kirkwood made arrangements for merchandising tie-ins to lure unpaid extras to the Sports Arena Monday. A foreign auto was to be raffled off, in exchange for a plug in the film, and other merchandise was to be given away at 15-minute intervals to keep the extras from leaving,” Variety reported during production. Extras were also given meals from Kentucky Fried Chicken, one background player recalled. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Adding to his injuries during filming, Stallone did break a rib during his final bout with Carl Weathers, while Weathers suffered a broken nose.

Did the studio really try to sabotage the production to get Stallone out as star?

Stallone pushed himself to run an estimated nine miles the first day of shooting and 11 the second, wearing Converse sneakers the whole time and giving himself a case of shin splints, according to the recent book “Going the Distance” about the making of “Rocky.” It’s not clear whether he was really told by doctors to stay off his feet for two weeks, as “I Play Rocky” shows.

But Kubik said that although the contract required a tight shooting schedule and budget, as well as giving producers the right to replace Stallone, it wouldn't have made much sense to get rid of him. “I knew if they were going to shoot half the movie with him, there was no way they were going to shoot for five days and then say we don’t like him,” said Kubik.

Stallone had a similar memory of the contract when talking to Howard Stern in 2005: “We have a 14-day thing where we can fire you any time and, more importantly, we can reduce it down to 900 grand, all in, and if you can do the thing in 30 days, OK. If not, it’s over.”

So although United Artists did write the contract with strict requirements in order to come in under budget, it wouldn’t have been in anyone’s interest to try to get Stallone to quit after shooting had already started.

Variety reported that director John Avildsen used numerous tactics to save money and come in under budget, including saving $200 by having Stallone provide voice work for three or four disguised voices issuing from bars and TV sets.

Did Stallone call his dad, Frank Stallone Sr., and ask him to appear in “Rocky?”

Sylvester Stallone had a difficult relationship with both his absentee mother and his abusive dad Frank Sr., who could never seem to show his approval no matter what Sly had accomplished. “I Play Rocky” shows him extending an olive branch by calling his dad and asking if he can play a small part as the man who rings the bell at the end of the boxing match. Is that how it really happened?

Not so much, Stallone recounts in his book “The Steps: A Memoir.” As he tells it, when he showed up on set to shoot a scene, Frank Sr. was already there waiting for him and insisted on being given a part. There was just one problem, Stallone says in his memoir: The part had already been cast. “There was no reasoning with him, so with apologies, I let go of the timekeeper,” he recalled. When it came time to shoot, Frank Jr. repeatedly missed his cue and didn't ring the bell, and the result was a “big Italian drama” of a fight, Stallone said .

articles.title: Searchlight Pictures Casting Head Yesi Ramirez Leaving Division Amid Restructuring
articles.summary: The ‘A Complete Unknown’ and ‘Moonlight’ casting director said in a statement that she will return to casting independently.
articles.content:
Yesi Ramirez, the head of casting for Searchlight Pictures , is departing the indie and specialty division after roughly six years.

The move comes amid a restructuring in the casting department at the Disney-owned division, which this year released films including Wild Horse Nine and Ready or Not 2: Here I Come , with Behemoth! and The Families Stone on the way.

In a statement, Ramirez said she would return to the world of independent casting after leaving the company. “I'll genuinely miss working alongside my Searchlight talented colleagues, many of whom have become dear friends. At the same time, I'm excited to return to independent casting, get back in the trenches with filmmakers, and be hands-on in discovering more talent and being creative,” she said. “It's a part of the work I've always loved, and I'm excited to get back to it." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies 'The Odyssey' to Receive Ensemble Performance Award at Palm Springs International Film Festival (Exclusive) Music Searchlight Pictures Enters Merch Partnership With Universal Music's Bravado (Exclusive)

At Searchlight, Ramirez oversaw the selection of actors on projects spanning the Oscar winner The Eyes of Tammy Faye as well as The Menu , Fire Island, Ready or Not and Ready or Not 2 , Rental Family and Flamin’ Hot. She personally cast the Bob Dylan biopic A Complete Unknown , advocating in particular for Monica Barbaro to play Joan Baez — a role for which Barbaro later earned an Oscar nomination.

Ramirez also personally cast the titles Chevalier , See How They Run and The Families Stone .

Prior to Disney purchasing 20th Century Fox, Ramirez led casting for three different film banners at the company and served as the casting director on The Hate U Give and The Art of Racing in the Rain .

Across her 20-year career in casting, Ramirez has worked on projects as varied as Blood Diamond, 21 Jump Street and Magic Mike XXL . She notably cast Barry Jenkins’ Oscar winner Moonlight , which earned her a 2017 Artios Award from Casting Society.

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday Just Got Confusing After Marvel Confirms X-Men Deleted Scene Is Canon
articles.summary: Disney - Marvel Is Channing Tatum's Gambit in Avengers: Doomsday the same one from Deadpool & Wolverine? If you ask Marvel boss Kevin Feige, the answer is yes. Marvel fans were beyond excited when it was originally confirmed that Tatum would return as the card-throwing, Cajun hero for the new Avengers movie, as he quickly became a fan […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Is Channing Tatum's Gambit in Avengers: Doomsday the same one from Deadpool & Wolverine ? If you ask Marvel boss Kevin Feige, the answer is yes . Marvel fans were beyond excited when it was originally confirmed that Tatum would return as the card-throwing, Cajun hero for the new Avengers movie , as he quickly became a fan favorite during the 2024 X-Men film, and that was after failing to play the role years prior . Now, though, it seems like his presence is about to be pretty confusing.

Speaking with Empire , Kevin Feige addressed whether the characters were the same with a sly confirmation, revealing: “[In Deadpool & Wolverine ] we see Channing look up, with a little sparkle in his eye that maybe he could get out of the Void, and clearly he does.” For Marvel fans, this reveal by Feige might be confusing, because the last time that we actually saw Tatum's Gambit in the movie was when the titular heroes were escaping The Void , and Gambit appeared to be swallowed up by Alioth. He wasn't alone either, with X-23 (Dafne Keen), Blade (Wesley Snipes), and Elektra (Jennifer Garner), all seemingly dying at the same time. A deleted scene tells a different story , though, and Marvel just confirmed it's canon to Avengers: Doomsday .

Though Marvel fans who only saw Deadpool & Wolverine in the theater may not recall this moment that Feige is talking about, die-hards who follow every crumb of MCU lore know exactly what he's talking about. Roughly a month after it was released, Deadpool & Wolverine star Ryan Reynolds revealed this specific moment in a post online, showing off a scene that confirmed Tatum's Gambit not only survived the deadly events seen in The Void but had escaped. Reynolds later confirmed that "a version of the sequence" is in the movie, but is buried "on one of the monitors in the deep background of the TVA." That said, it begs two major questions.

*whispers* Marvel Sparkle Circle #DeadpoolAndWolverine ❤️💛 pic.twitter.com/TtuZ5jSAdL

The first question that this scene forces us to ponder is…who opened the portal for Gambit to escape from? Originally, the Sling Ring portal was opened in the film by Cassandra Nova, and since she gets ripped apart by the end of the movie, it's not her. Perhaps Deadpool himself saved Gambit from The Void, but this brings up the second major question: What the heck happened to X-23 , Blade, and Elektra? Deciding that a deleted scene is canon doesn't feel that out of left field for Marvel, even if they claim that the footage can be seen in the movie (one assumes it requires a microscope to witness), but it leaves a major hole open about the status of beloved Marvel superheroes in the process.

Perhaps a throwaway line in Avengers: Doomsday will settle this all, but given the magnitude of the storytelling and the sheer number of characters, Marvel is probably just expecting fans to go with it when they get in the theater. What do you think? Is it fine that Marvel decided a deleted scene was canon and we should all just go with it? Or is Marvel having its cajun cake and eating it too?

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google One of the biggest consistencies in the Persona series is how long it takes for mainline titles to come out, with the nine year gap between Persona 5 and Persona 6 only growing. However, Atlus has shared a new strategy to reduce the time between mainline Persona games, primarily between Persona 6 when it comes out and an eventual Persona 7 . This could bring the franchise back to its Persona 3 or Persona 4 days, where it only took a couple of years to advance the series forward rather than taking huge breaks to release multiple spin-offs over the course of nearly a decade.

A developer interview with Persona series general producer Kazuhisa Wada discussed how the franchise is expanding overseas, talking to "SegaSammyMania" as part of a multi-part talk on the subject. Toward the end of the interview, Wada explains how Persona 6 isn't the endpoint of the series, and instead is more of a new process to turn the franchise into an even bigger IP. The "brainstorming of creative ideas and developments" for Persona 6 and beyond seems to be a big priority for Atlus, especially after the recent success of their last title — Metaphor: ReFantazio .

According to Wada, "We're [Atlus] taking various measures to ensure that fans won't have to wait as long for the next installment as in the past," indicating that Persona 7 could launch within a few years of Persona 6 's release. Currently, it is unclear what the release window of Persona 6 might be, but many player theorize that as more information comes out, the title could be a mid to late 2027 title. In the past, the launch of Persona 6 would mean that the game would be the center of all Persona content for several years, reflecting the long time between mainline entries that has become the franchise standard.

Atlus seems to be realizing that players might grow out of the target demographic for Persona games if it takes them nearly 10 years to come out, even if spin-offs keep one title's characters, setting, and themes alive. With excitement for Persona 6 being high due to its mysterious status, perhaps Atlus wants to keep the incoming audience by making the series progress without as much wait. Further comments by Wada say that "to improve development efficiency, we are strengthening collaboration between [internal] departments and improving the development process by utilizing management and sharing tools."

While this is very savvy business-speak, Wada is referring to the three internal studios that make up Atlus, including:

By consolidating resources between all three groups, the most talented creators on all Atlus teams can contribute their talent toward the best Persona games possible. Cooperation has always been present in these groups, but official shared work between them could accelerate production of Persona works fast. Wada went on to also say that "we place great importance on sharing core values in development," meaning that the best ideas from all departments are something Atlus shares between their projects. Some of those ideas and values were listed to be "taking initiative, understanding and helping each other, embracing change while enjoying it, and breaking through preconceived notions."

Shared values between teams for Persona 6 or Persona 7 could allow Atlus to have a singular focus on the series. This could not only let Persona 7 use some of the same game-making techniques and assets from Persona 6 's production, but also let developers stay familiar with what the series need to evolve. Wada continues the interview mentioned earlier by claiming "we can reduce inconsistencies in judgment and focus our efforts on what truly matters" and "we are reviewing the very mechanism of product creation, looking beyond just a single product to future development."

Through this newfound collaboration, which has honestly been within Atlus since the production of Metaphor: ReFantazio , Persona doesn't have to rely on one person to have a consistent vision either. Training young staff is obviously a part to this, but considering how many Persona team members have already worked hard with Studio Zero on Metaphor: ReFantazio , the environment of the studio couldn't be more geared toward cooperation. Perhaps this confidence in how the team has worked on successful games like Metaphor has inspired Atlus to commit to a smaller gap between Persona games, or in Wada's words, "as the overall level of the team rises, the level of the leaders will naturally rise as well."

Unlike the gap between Persona 4 and Persona 5 , Atlus isn't suffering the financial disaster of its parent company that threatens the survival of their IPs. As Wada talks about how "it's essential fore all staff members to have a high level of awareness and perspective," it's exciting to think about how the Persona series will have more staff and resources to reduce its notorious break between mainline games. While we know frustratingly few details about Persona 6 right now, the fact that Atlus is describing it as a series advancement rather than its end is promising for the franchise's biggest fans.

articles.title: I Didn't Think It Would Take A Doc To Get Amanda Seyfried On SNL, But I Love Her 'Sweet' Response
articles.summary: Let her eat cake.
articles.content:
Amanda Seyfried busted onto the Hollywood scene on soaps in the Noughties, but it was her role in Mean Girls in 2005 that made her a household name. Since then, she’s been in a ton of huge movie and TV roles including Les Miserablès , The Dropout , Big Love , Jennifer’s Body , Dear John , Mamma Mia! and The Housemaid . Not one of these roles led her to landing on the relatively rare list names to ever host SNL . That is, until You Can See Everything came around.

I mean "sweet" in the literal sense. While we know Seyfried can be funny ( it’s like she has ESPN or something ), she does seem a little nervous about taking the stage at Studio 8h, and asked her fans and pals to “send cake.”

If you are a fan of the actress, you may already know she’s a noted cake lover. She turned 40 during The Housemaid ’s promotional tour, and there were so many viral cake moments, including one where she pretty much murdered a cake with a knife. Yes, it was fittingly on brand.

Getting a cake on your birthday is kind of fun, but cake actually has a special place in the actress' heart. She talked about this love of cake with Harper’s Bazaar once, so it’s a real thing.

I’m genuinely excited for Amanda Seyfried to expand her abilities and to give the late night series a whirl. It's a special rite of passage for a lot of Hollywood, and hey, if she's good, maybe one day she'll even enter the coveted Five Timers Club ! Regardless, if you told me all this would have happened because of a literal documentary, I'm not sure I would have believed you.

articles.title: Rockstar Games Boss Fires Back at Questions About GTA 7
articles.summary: After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is now finally live around the globe. Arguably the most eagerly anticipated game in history, most who are playing GTA 6 are surely nowhere close to finishing it, as Rockstar's latest boasts hundreds of hours' worth of content to dig into. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is now finally live around the globe. Arguably the most eagerly anticipated game in history, most who are playing GTA 6 are surely nowhere close to finishing it, as Rockstar's latest boasts hundreds of hours' worth of content to dig into . Despite this, some have already started to think ahead, specifically with Grand Theft Auto 7 and what it might end up looking like. And if you feel like it already might be a bit too early to look forward to GTA 7 , one of the key bosses in charge of the series would agree.

Speaking on TBPN , Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick was asked about Grand Theft Auto 7 and what it might have in store. While Rockstar's world in GTA 6 is drastically larger than anything else the studio has ever done , Zelnick was asked if the next entry in the series could take place around the entire globe rather than in one region. Rather than entertaining this idea at all, Zelnick kept the focus on GTA 6 , suggesting that they've not even begun to think even a little about GTA 7 .

"We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on November 19th," Zelnick said. "Wait, let me check my watch. Oh, it's still November 19th. And you're asking a question about GTA 7 . I mean, guys, really?"

Jordi: "Theoretically, GTA 7 could just be a live version of the entire world, right?" @StraussZelnick , the CEO behind GTA 6: "We went live with GTA 6 on November 19. Let me check my watch. Oh, it's still November 19. And you're asking a question about GTA 7." https://t.co/Up2ILZaP5t pic.twitter.com/3fgFISHqgy

You can't blame Zelnick for having this reaction for a number of reasons. Not only do those at Rockstar Games surely have no idea what Grand Theft Auto 7 might look like right now, but their work on GTA 6 has truly only just begun. While the single-player component of GTA 6 is live now, it's expected that a new version of GTA Online will come to the game in the future . This will give GTA 6 a live-service aspect that will continue to take up a good amount of Rockstar's focus in the years to come.

The good news with GTA 7 is that Rockstar should be able to continue going bigger and better than before with the next installment in the series. GTA 6 sales have already been confirmed to have topped 32 million units , with Rockstar and Take-Two having made nearly $4 billion on the first day of the game's launch. This makes GTA 6 the most successful entertainment release in history, and will undoubtedly give Rockstar plenty of resources at its disposal whenever it does decide to make the next Grand Theft Auto game.

How do you feel about GTA 6 based on what you may have played so far? And do you think there's still room for improvement with GTA 7 ? Let me know in the comments below.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Hunger Games movie franchise is returning to theaters this week with the prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping , which provides much deeper backstory and context for the original Hunger Games book (and film), as well as its sequel, Catching Fire . As the franchise comes full circle, the former stars of the original Hunger Games movie franchise (Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Woody Harrelson) have been back in the spotlight. Hutcherson has been particularly interesting to hear from, as he is currently in the developmental pipeline over at DC Studios, where he is set to play the character Scott Free (aka Mister Miracle) in an upcoming adult animated series that's set for release in 2028.

Of course, there have been some pretty seismic shakeups over at DC Studios in the last few weeks: After Warner Bros. merged with Skydance, James Gunn and Peter Safran were asked to step down from the leadership position of DC Studios and were replaced by Jeremy Latcham. Rumors are swirling that DC Studios could got through a major change of creative direction, and that old plans may not still pan out.

If you don't already know, DC's Mister Miracle animated series will be an adaptation of writer Tom King and artist Mitch Gerads' Mister Miracle comic series, which for 12 issues from 2017-2019. The comic follows Scott Free/Mister Miracle, the universe's greatest escape artist, and his wife, the cosmic warrior Big Barda, as they try to live a domestic life on Earth, but find that the escalating war between their homeworlds of New Genesis and Apokolips demands their attention and action. However, Scott's nightmare past (adopted and raised by Apokolips' ruler, Darkseid) and deep doubts about his seemingly immortal life take him down a very dark path of mental health struggles, in addition ot the battles he has to fight as a dad and Mister Miracle.

Josh Hutcherson will play Scott Free/Mister Miracle, and Mackenzie Davis ( Terminator: Dark Fate ) will play Big Barda in the Mister Miracle animated series. While speaking with Josh Horowitz's Happy Sad Confused podcast , Hutcherson addressed his DCU role and confirmed that it won't just be a voice-acting performance: he is set to play Mister Miracle in live-action as well.

"This [ Mister Miracle ] was like a very extensive auditioning process," Hutcherson told Horowitz. "Because whoever plays them in the animated version will play them in the live-action version. So that's the plan. That's the track that we're trying to follow. Tom King, who wrote the comics, is phenomenal. He was our showrunner as well, so he knows it inside and out. He knows Scott Free/Mister Miracle inside and out. And getting to have Mackenzie Davis there with me as well, to play Big Barda. She was amazing. That was just such a great project."

Hutcherson made sure to let DC fans know that this isn't just another acting job: he bonded with the character in such a big way that it probably helped him land the job.

"Mister Miracle came around, and I read. All I had was a few of the scenes to do the audition. And it was such a cool character, and then I started getting into the comics and reading through those, and the world is amazing. What it talks about with mental health and all of that, I think, is something that's very special, and I'm honored to be Scott Free, and I can't wait," Hutcherson later added. "I think that Mr. Miracle is such a great character, such an amazing story… I can't wait for people to see the show."

Mister Miracle is expected to be released on HBO Max in 2028.

articles.title: "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return
articles.summary: Screenwriter Billy Ray, producer Nina Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence reveal how they adapted Suzanne Collins’ prequel before it was published, found their young Haymitch and brought back Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson.
articles.content:
Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’ s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

Before the odds could be in their favor, the creative team behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had to survive a Games of their own, one played entirely in secret.

The rules were simple: one copy of the book, no internet and not a word to anyone. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Hunts Down $21M in Box Office Previews Movies Jennifer Lawrence Thinks Her 'Hunger Games' Bow and Arrow Prop Was Stolen

When Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins called her trusted adapters, director Francis Lawrence , producer Nina Jacobson and original Hunger Games screenwriter Billy Ray , they were eager to read her new story. The catch: it wasn’t fully finished, and it hadn’t been announced to the public. That meant caution was essential. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Take Ray’s process for example. The screenwriter didn’t write his latest Hunger Games script on his own computer. Each day, he drove onto the Fox lot to Jacobson’s office and sat down in a small room with a safe that guarded Collins' story. An assistant opened the safe, took out a laptop that had never been connected to the internet and set it in front of him. He wrote all day, said “Done,” and the laptop went back into the safe.

“That’s how the script got written, which of course I had never done before,” Ray tells The Hollywood Reporter .

It was an unusual way to adapt a novel that almost no one outside that small circle knew existed, yet maintaining strict confidentiality was imperative given the phenomenon Collins’ franchise has become. The original four films — The Hunger Games , Catching Fire and Mockingjay Part 1 and 2 — grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide. Debuting with its first book in 2008, the dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat has grown into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history. Across its five installments, the series has sold more than 100 million copies globally. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In 2020, Collins released her first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , which chronicled the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow. The film was adapted for feature film starring Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler. Now with Sunrise on the Reaping , released on Nov. 20, Collins has returned to another familiar face: Haymitch Abernathy, the District 12 mentor Woody Harrelson played in the films.

The prequel revisits the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games , starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, when a younger Haymitch (portrayed by Joseph Zada ) competes. Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, where the traditional choice of one male and one female from a district has been doubled to two of each.

Though initially not among the four selected tributes for District 12, Haymitch is automatically volunteered as punishment for trying to protect his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) who reacts after one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by Capitol soldiers known as "Peacekeepers."

The Haymitch origin story answers a question fans have had since the first film: how the hopeful, mischievous kid became the bitter, drunken mentor to Jennifer Lawrence 's Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson 's Peeta Mellark that Harrelson played.

Ahead of the film’s release, Ray, Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence spoke with THR about working under an NDA bubble, finding their new Haymitch and reuniting franchise alums Harrelson, Lawrence and Hutcherson. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When The Hunger Games was first adapted for the screen, screenwriter Ray and director Gary Ross launched what would grow into a global success. Since both Ray and Ross parted ways with the franchise following the initial installment, Ray's comeback to craft the backstory for a character he helped popularize represented a complete full-circle experience.

"Having launched that franchise, The Hunger Games has been such a blessing in my career," Ray tells THR . "I can't begin to enumerate all the ways it's been great for me."

"When the opportunity came to come back, I said yes before I read the book," he says of his return. "It was something I wanted to do. I wanted to work with Francis, and I wanted to be back under the hood with Suzanne and with Nina."

Ray has stayed close with Collins, who read an early draft of his debut novel, Burn the Water , which was released earlier this year. "It was as if we had spoken the day before," he says of reteaming with Collins and others for Sunrise on the Reaping . "There was just no falloff at all."

When Collins calls, producer Jacobson, director Lawrence and Ray answer, ready to find out what the author has created this time. But her first question is always the same: "Why don't you guys take a look and let me know if you think it's a movie?"

"This is always kind of hilarious… We read this one and said, 'Yeah, it's a movie, Suzanne,'" Lawrence says, laughing. Jacobson's answer was just as immediate: "My first response was, 'Hell yes.'" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Collins' question is a sincere one, though, Lawrence explains. "She's very serious when she says it's OK to tell her it's not a movie. When you create anything, you're vulnerable, and when she hands something to us, it's usually not completely finished. She feels vulnerable about it and wants some reassurance that it really is worthy of being on the screen."

Getting that far took some doing. When the team read an early draft of The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , the world was in lockdown, so keeping it secret was easier, Lawrence says. Sunrise on the Reaping brought "a different kind of tension, because the book had not yet been published, so the secrecy and security around the project was pretty extreme," Ray says.

"For us, the secrecy was insane," Jacobson says. "We had one hard copy of the book. It had to be mailed or messengered from New York to L.A. in sections. First it lived at her [Collins'] agent's house and then eventually we got a safe for my office and it moved into the safe. There was one copy, and people could make an appointment if they needed to read it."

The secrecy extended to casting, too. "Even once we had our script, we couldn't release sides, or even use a scene from the book instead of sides, because if we read an actor, people would know what scenes and characters were in the book besides Haymitch," Jacobson says. "So we had the young actors do improvs, just so we could get acquainted with this generation of actors and start to collect knowledge about who they are." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Having to keep it locked down in this NDA bubble was exciting," she adds. "It was sort of stressful, and I was incredibly relieved when we could finally talk about it!"

"We knew Haymitch was going to be the trickiest person to cast, because we're anchored with him," Lawrence says.

Joseph Zada, who starred in Prime Video's We Were Liars and had filmed Netflix's East of Eden series, caught the attention of casting directors Debra Zane and Dylan Jury, who wanted Lawrence and Jacobson to meet him.

"He had sent in an improv tape. We had many, many people do improv tapes just to see who was out in the world, and his was pretty special," Lawrence recalls.

From there, the audition process became its own Hunger Games. "We really put him through the wringer in the audition process," the director admits. "We tested and tested to make sure he would be emotionally capable of going through everything he needed to go through, that he had the sense of mischief and irreverence Woody has, and that he could embody all those characteristics without feeling like he was doing an impression. That was the tricky thing. But he was definitely the guy."

"We needed to know he had the range to experience all of the loss in the movie, and to do it in different ways: sometimes shame, guilt or anger, or just complete loss and grief," Lawrence adds. "We needed somebody who could bring all of that." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For Jacobson, the deciding quality was mischief. "You needed somebody who had mischief in them, and that's a surprisingly hard thing to find," she says. "There are some wonderful, likable actors who are very capable leading men, but who don't necessarily have that mischief in them, that troublemaker vibe. And yet at his young age, it can't be that dark, twisted kind of mischief-maker or trickster. It's a boyish quality."

Zada was someone who "had a hopeful, sunny disposition" and the mischief they wanted Haymitch to embody.

"When you first meet him in the original movies, you don't understand why he's so angry, drunken, broken and bitter. You assume, well, it can't be easy being a mentor for the poorest, most disadvantaged district out there," she continues. "What all of us wanted to see in this one, and what Joseph captured so beautifully, is that he was bright, funny, hopeful and very apolitical."

Zada's chemistry with Peak, cast as his love interest, Lenore Dove, sealed it. "You just felt it. You felt like this woman is the woman he loves. She's his best friend. She's the person who makes it all make sense for him," Jacobson says of their chemistry reads together.

"There's a quality about Woody, and we had to find someone who had that quality but wasn't going to get burdened by it," she says. "With all of our actors, we always said, 'We don't want impersonation. We want interpretation.'"

That philosophy extended well beyond Haymitch. From Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning to Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons and Ralph Fiennes, Sunrise wasn't short on A-listers joining its younger, newer cast members that also included Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, Molly McCann and Percy Daggs IV. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But joining an established franchise isn't always an immediate yes, Jacobson says. "There are definitely some people who just don't know the series that well, so it's about educating them about it, and making sure they know we're not looking for them to impersonate," she explains. "We want their interpretation of the character. If they don't know the series, oftentimes they have to go ask around a bit and talk to people in their lives."

Culkin and Fanning, who play Caesar Flickerman and Effie Trinket, have been candid about finding their own interpretations while respecting the characters Stanley Tucci and Elizabeth Banks originated.

"What we tell people who are new to it, and I really do believe this quite earnestly, is that it's one of the very few franchises where, for each of the renowned actors we cast, it is actually all about performance. It's never about prosthetics or visual effects," Jacobson says. (Well, almost never: "Of course we use those things sparingly here and there. Those are not Glenn's teeth," she notes.)

The appeal, she says, is the creative freedom that comes with everything being "rooted in performance." "You're going to be collaborating closely with Francis and the department heads on the creation, building and design of your character, and it's going to come down to meaty character work. You're very rarely against a green screen. You're almost always in a practical location with, hopefully, some other amazing actors in the scenes with you. I think these movies give each actor a real showcase of their talents, in a way that isn't always true in a lot of other franchises." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid7' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Jacobson recalls Sunrise on the Reaping being an "incredibly emotional" read. "I cried quite a few times, and then cried quite a lot at the end. I found it so fully moving and satisfying on so many levels."

But how do you adapt a book fans haven't been able to read yet? The creative team relied on being fans themselves.

"Nina and I consider ourselves fans, so there are a lot of things we fight to keep from the book, details we love ourselves," Lawrence says. "And Suzanne is obviously going to fight for certain things: making sure her themes, ideas, the spirit of the characters and their emotional arcs are there. So there's a good group of us there to protect what we think fans are going to love."

"The funny thing is, it's incredibly easy for me to know how fans will feel, because I'm the OG fan," Jacobson says. "I'm as obsessed with the books as any diehard fan, and so is Francis."

Still, some things had to go. "If I put everything that's in the book into the movie, the movie would be six hours long. You can't do that," Ray says.

Sunrise doubles the number of tributes competing in the Games, and the team knew they couldn't explore every one in depth. "Getting to know the tributes and understanding potential allies and enemies is one of the parts of these movies people really enjoy and are invested in. So figuring out how to balance the 48, and making sure we gave time and attention to the core characters whose stories are connected to Haymitch's journey, was a definite challenge," Jacobson says. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid8' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The book is also told entirely from Haymitch's point of view, which posed its own challenge. "What we found even in the original movies with Katniss was that if she wasn't in a scene, the scene still needed to be about her in some way," Jacobson says. "But when you're only ever with that one person, there's important context and opportunities you might miss. So figuring out where to break with his point of view, when to show something he can't see or know, was a big decision in the adaptation process."

As for every other decision, the guiding principle was Collins.

"At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, 'What is this book about for you?'" Ray recalls. "She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume and John Locke. And I said, 'Suzanne, what's the book about for you emotionally?' She said, 'It's about love and loss.' I said, 'Great, that's what I'm writing.' So anything that didn't stick to that had to go."

The Haymitch audiences meet in Sunrise is a far cry from the broken alcoholic of the original films. In Sunrise , audiences encounter a teen initially easygoing and unconcerned with politics. But his life transforms when he is forced into the 50th Hunger Games. Refusing to simply comply, he attempts to disrupt the Capitol's system and oppose President Snow, altering both his own destiny and the world around him. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid9' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Jacobson likens the young Haymitch to the "kind of guy who's probably not very serious about school and is just waiting for the end of the day to run down to the beach with his surfboard and his girlfriend, hang out and catch some waves." His attitude, as she sees it: "I can't do anything about this broken world that I live in, but I've got a girl I love and a family I love, and that's enough for me. Who am I? What difference would I make anyway?"

Jacobson sees Haymitch's arc as similar to Katniss', with a priority on family that grows to include their community and district. "Your circle of concern grows in each movie, and there's a cost to expanding that circle, a price to pay… But it's the things he hears and brings with him from Lenore Dove. He says the Capitol has all the power and always will, and she says that doesn't mean they always have, and it doesn't mean they always will. It's this notion that it's not a foregone conclusion that oppressive power structures can't be disrupted and ultimately destroyed."

The Haymitch of the film faces a dilemma: "What am I willing to give up for the people I care about? And what am I willing to give up to right these really profound wrongs and try to end the Games?"

"Seeing him get radicalized, and seeing him decide, even with all this loss, that the way to honor these people is to continue to fight: that was what was really important to me, and what I found really interesting and moving," Lawrence says.

"You see Haymitch in the other movies, and Woody does an amazing job portraying him, but people laugh with him," the director adds. "He's a drunk, and you just don't know the history. Now you follow this movie and see all that he went through, how long and hard he fought, all the years he had to escort tributes to the arena and watch them die. But he continued to fight and kept his promise to his girlfriend, his mother, his brother, to Maysilee (portrayed by Grace) and all of them." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid10' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For Ray, filling in that history was the point. "In that first movie, obviously Haymitch is just broken, with a real serious drinking problem and a lot of pain. This was the movie that explained all that, and it was great to do that sort of history retroactively, to say, 'This explains the behavior you've been seeing through all those movies,'" he says. "People know what happened, and the trick is saying, 'Here's the part you didn't know.' That's what we were going for here."

Collins doesn't write unless she has something to say, and themes have been the foundation of each Hunger Games book. With the original trilogy, she explored the consequences of war for teens. With the prequels, she continues to examine the state of the world.

"Look at the themes she's dealing with now and how relevant they are: there's a bit of a call to action, this idea of implicit submission, and diving into the use of propaganda to get people to submit. So there are fresh ideas that feel very relevant. There's meat on the bone," Lawrence says. "Take this idea of implicit submission. You can look at any government, whether it's authoritarian, fascist or one that calls itself democratic: as humans, we always agree to be ruled by the few. It's a bit of a call to action: don't be apathetic, stand up, voice your beliefs, and don't expect instant gratification, because change may take time. I feel that's very relevant now, but it's also timeless, because people are constantly fighting for their rights. You see it in Hungary, with the ousting of a regime, and in Brazil, where people actually make change. That's happening now, but it's also something that's been happening for thousands of years." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid11' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Ray says he approached both the original film and Sunrise as if they were "true stories."

"And they're getting closer and closer to being that, which is the bad news for us as a culture, and the great news for Suzanne Collins, because she has her finger on the pulse of something, and it does feel like a true story. If you think of it that way, you can write it as a screenwriter from a place of complete outrage," he says.

Haymitch's journey matters now even more given it's "a time when so many people feel like, 'What's the point of trying to make a difference?'" Jacobson says. "It's a story that is so emotional about how hard it is to try to make a difference. It's also about how what you set in motion today might not be realized for another generation, and how hard it is to continue to resist and to endure, knowing that the changes you hope for could take 25 years to accomplish."

Anyone who knows The Hunger Games knows the brutality of the story. "I think an audience that has bought into the concept that a government forces children to kill each other knows they're coming to see something dark," Ray says. "I don't think anybody is going to come away saying, 'Wow, I was expecting a musical. What the hell is this?'"

Even so, certain sequences in Sunrise had to be toned down to keep the film's PG-13 rating. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid12' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"There's a moment in the book where a character is holding the head of a child, and I thought, 'We're never going to be able to do that.' There were probably three moments in the book where I went, 'Come on, Suzanne, this is never going to happen.' And she understands that when we get into the process," Lawrence says.

The story's emotional darkness stayed intact, and Lawrence says it was "toughest" on Zada, who had to ride that roller coaster on set.

"Whenever we led up to certain days, whether it was a Lenore Dove scene or a Maysilee scene, it was always a little scary for him, because he knew he'd have to sit in those feelings for 10 or 12 hours, basically all day," he says.

The Games were filmed first, with the District 12 scenes shot later. "He was so happy to just be happy: going to work convinced he'd never get called in the reaping, having a nice scene in the meadow with Lenore Dove, being in the candy shop. He looked forward to those days," Lawrence says.

But the darker turns were never far off. "We also had to do things like shoot his and Lenore Dove's first scene one day and then, because we were in that location, jump to the end the very next day and do that whole scene (readers know the one.) That was tough on Joe. Even when he was happy to be happy, he knew what was coming tomorrow. That weighed on him more than it did on me," the director says.

Though the book and film follow a younger Haymitch, the book's epilogue, featuring Katniss, Peeta and an older Haymitch, was in the script from the start. "It was such a profound honor to get to write those characters again. It was just pure joy," Ray says. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid13' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"I remember reading the epilogue in the manuscript and thinking, 'Wow, this is fantastic.' I found it really moving," Lawrence says of the trio's return in the book.

"The hope was always to bring them back," the director says of Harrelson, Hutcherson and Jennifer Lawrence. But because of the secrecy surrounding the book and the adaptation, "We didn't reach out to them until, I want to say, the day before the announcement. That's when I called the three of them."

While the team hoped for an immediate yes, they prepared in case scheduling conflicts or other circumstances kept the actors from returning. "We had already tasked ourselves with figuring out how to make the story as fulfilling as possible if it didn't happen," Lawrence says.

But there was no need to rethink the epilogue: the actors were "all very excited to return," he says. "Then it was really just a scheduling question: when can we get the three of them together and out to Germany?" the director says.

Francis Lawrence has stayed in touch with the cast, but working together again in the world of The Hunger Games made for an especially meaningful reunion. "I think it was a Wednesday night when they arrived, and I got a text from Jen that she and Josh were having a beer in the hotel bar. I was coming back from set, so I joined, then Nina joined, and our cinematographer, the still photographer, the sound mixer… It's the same group of people who have been making these movies for 16 years, so we had this great reunion of about 30 of us before costume fittings and all of that." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid14' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

With two prequel novels and films now out, the question is always whether there are more stories to tell in Panem. The creative team admits they're just as in the dark as everyone else.

"She only really writes when she has something to say, so I hope she has something she wants to write about in this world, because I would miss it a lot," Jacobson says.

Fans have been quick to name the characters they'd love to follow in their early years, with Finnick (portrayed by Sam Claflin) and Johanna (Jena Malone) at the top of the list, along with the first Hunger Games. After Sunrise , Jacobson's own fascination is Plutarch. "When I realized from this book that Plutarch has been playing a double agent for 25 years by the time you meet him in Catching Fire , that to me is pretty fascinating. How do you pull that off? How could you possibly live that close to such danger? And what compromises did you have to make? He is not a morally clean character at all, so I have a total fascination with him," she says.

If the prequels have proved anything, it's to never say never, a lesson Jacobson says the team learned early. "When we finished the original trilogy of books, we really thought we were done. We've never tried to make a movie without a book of hers. We only make her books. We never tried to develop anything that wasn't based on something she had given us as a book she was going to publish. So when we first got Ballad , all of a sudden it was, 'Oh my god, we're coming back to this world.'" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid15' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"I was so wowed by the way she's taken us on this journey, and by the amount of things that come together in this movie from all of the books and all of the movies. On the other hand, honestly, you could make this [ Sunrise ] the first book you've ever read, or the first movie you've seen. You could start here, make it your jumping-off point, and then go in any order you wanted. So there's accessibility for everyone."

As for future stories, Lawrence and Jacobson are hopeful but note only Collins will know the answer.

"I don't know if 'superstitious' is the right word, but she really does not let on whether or not she's writing," Lawrence says of Collins. "If she gets an idea and works on it, she keeps quiet, then turns it in to her publisher, who she trusts immensely, and waits to hear that it's a publishable book. Only then does she tell us she's written something."

"I have not heard anything. Would I love her to write another book? Yes, I sure would, because I still love the world so much, and I still find there's so much to learn," Jacobson says. "Because she digs so deep in terms of both history and philosophy, I hope she still has so much more to say, and I hope she'll decide to say it in Panem. But I don't know. We haven't gotten any winks or nods yet. I hope I get a wink and a nod, but I have gotten no winks, no nods so far."

articles.summary: A-1 Pictures The 2010s were filled with a lot of brief, but impactful anime series. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The 2010s were filled with a lot of brief, but impactful anime series. A lot of modern notable hits got their start in the 2010s, but some of the most notable ones from the decade were anime that were only given 24 episodes or less.

The 2010s were an era when even the more underground anime were being put on to streaming services. This resulted in a lot of smaller shows gaining interest and popularity by fans of the genre. It was an exploratory time where western anime fans were finally free to find other anime, and explore genres they may like. If you weren’t expanding your horizons during this time, then you may not have heard of some of the anime on this list.

The story of this anime and the themes it tackles still hit hard to this day. A group of childhood friends have grown apart after the death of one of their close friends, Meiko Honma, five years ago. Jinta Yadomi starts to be haunted by the ghost of his dead friend as she tries to figure out how to pass on into the afterlife. Yadomi begins to track down the old friend group so they can share their memories of Honma to determine what her last wish might have been.

The anime approaches the topic of torn friendships and childhood regret. It puts a cast of imperfect characters on display whose methods of coping feel realistic. The characters have all grown since five years ago, but they are still flawed and it shows. This anime shows the different ways in which people put on masks to hide their feelings. Each of the characters hides the trauma of losing their friend in different ways. As the series progresses, Yadomi (with Honma’s help) begins to bring them back together by getting to the root of why they fell apart in the first place. All the while they are still trying to help Honma pass on to the afterlife.

The story follows 17 year old Shinichi Izumi, whose hand is taken over by a powerful alien parasite. Shinichi learns that the parasite was actually after his brain, and that many other dangerous parasites also exist on earth. The parasites seek to inhabit a human host to then turn into horrifying flesh weapons and feed on other humans. Shinichi names his new parasite Migi, and together they work to protect other humans from falling victim to the parasites.

This anime has the perfect balance of horror and action throughout as Shinichi has to discover what the parasites are planning and confront them using his own powers. There are themes in the series like body and psychological horror, and also asks the question of what it means to be human as Shinichi finds his personality fading more the background as he and Migi grow stronger together.

The Disastrous Life of Saiki K was an iconic parody anime of the 2010s airing at an ideal time for the comedy it conveyed. The parody comedy in this one lent itself well to the environment of popular anime of the time. There are so many tropes that the anime pokes fun at in various genres. At the same time, there are plenty of fun jokes that work well on their own as well.

Kusuo Saiki is a near omniscient boy with many powers, including telepathy and telekinesis. The anime takes this grand concept and places Saiki in a normal high school where he works on solving problems without revealing himself. Every episode there is a new minor conflict that Saiki struggles to solve despite his powers. The set ups for the jokes, and the characters themselves, are hilarious. The comedy still holds up too as it's the sort of anime whose simple but fun comedy never ages.

Along with Steins;Gate , Erased was one of the most recognizable mystery anime of the 2010s, and it is still a gem to this day. There wasn’t really anything like it at the time, and its story had viewers of the anime on the edge of their seat all the way until the finale.

The story follows 29 year old Satoru Fujinuma, a part-time pizza delivery driver living in Chiba, Japan. When he finds his mother murdered in their home, he is sent back 18 years in the past to stop the events that led up to it. What follows is an episodic story that requires you to remember small details as both Satoru and the viewer try to discover what significance his childhood has in preventing his mother’s murder. The mystery plot of this 2010s anime is one of the most engaging that you can find to this day.

Along with Anohana , Your Lie in April was another big tearjerker anime of the 2010s. The anime tackles things like trauma and abuse while also having a gorgeous soundtrack and visuals. The story follows Kosei Arima, a former piano prodigy who has lost the will to play. He was once a well-known pianist who reached his skill level because of his abusive mother’s strict teaching. After his mother dies, he finds himself unable to even hear the sound of the piano when he plays it. He meets a young girl named Kaori Miyazono who slowly but surely begins to break down his walls and give him the courage to play for himself again.

The anime tackles surprisingly mature themes like trauma and grief. It shows the sorts of pressure that people striving to be the best are put under, and just how brutal the road to excellence can be. Kosei’s journey to begin playing again is very satisfying to watch, and the side characters in the series support the story in positive ways. There is a bit of romance in the anime, but the main draw is Kosei’s and Kaori’s difficult journeys as they both grapple with circumstances that try to prevent them from playing again.

What anime do you remember fondly from the 2010s? Are there lesser known 2010s hits that people should know of? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
